newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Nationals happier with Canberra's native land plan.
newsitem.headline: Nationals happier with Canberra's native land plan.

text.p: The rural-based National Party, part of Australia's ruling coalition, moderated its hostility to the government's native title plan on Wednesday.
National Party President Don McDonald said Liberal Prime Minister John Howard had assured him that the government's planned system to regulate the thorny issue would meet its concerns.
Howard said he had made no substantial concessions in the plan, which his cabinet had endorsed earlier, as expected.
Until Wednesday, trenchant National Party opposition to Howard's plans threatened a split in the ruling coalition.

The National Party's parliamentary leaders meanwhile maintained cabinet solidarity on Wednesday and defended government policy, which rejects National Party demands to simply seek outright legislative extinguishment of rights that the High Court gave Aborigines last year.
McDonald said he and the national's two parliamentary leaders, Deputy Prime Minister Tim Fischer and Primary Industries Minister John Anderson, had met Howard on Wednesday.

"I can say that considerable progress was made towards strengthening what will emerge within the detail of the Wik response to achieve the bottom line objective of the National Party," he said in a statement.
The "bottom line objective" is certainty for farmers, who say they cannot make business decisions until the government ensures that Aborigines cannot interfere with their operations.
In theory parliament could achieve this with legislation that abolishes the rights to share land leased to pastoralists, granted by court in December in the Wik case.
But such extreme action would appear racist, and the Federal government would have to compensate Aborigines for any property rights it took away.
Instead the government wants to minimise the Aboriginal rights only as far as needed to protect primary production. It would also create a smooth system for land-rights claims.
McDonald said the National Party still wanted extinguishment but the party's parliamentary leaders backed government policy.
The court ruled last year that leases giving the pastoralist exclusive occupancy of the land were unaffected, and Anderson said in a statement that other leases would be sufficiently protected.
Fischer told reporters that the plan was the best and fairest solution to the issue.
